Warm-up
what the stages mean
RAISEGet warm and get blood moving — the jog, or the opening kilometre of an easy run.
MOVETake the joints you are about to load through their range, and wake the muscles that hold them.
PRIMEThe last step before the work: strides before a hard run, ramp-up sets before a lift. The one most people skip. Called potentiation.
×8-10Reps. 30s is a hold. /side means that each way, not in total.
Cooldown
what the stages mean
ROLLFoam roller or ball on the tissue — slow, pausing where it is sore. Takes the edge off before you move it.
MOVEThrough the range under your own control, no holding. Restores the range the session used up. Called dynamic stretching.
HOLDSettle into the stretch and stay there for the time given. This is the one that adds range, and the reason it comes last. Called static stretching.

Where do these progressions come from?
Pull-up, push-up, pistol, dip and handstand progressions come from coaching consensus. Muscle-up is a reasonable extension, not directly sourced — marked with an asterisk.
Mobility Skills
what you're chasing, and where each one sits
Where do these progressions come from?
Pike, bridge, front-split and middle-split are independently verified against real studies. Pancake, deep squat and overhead squat are reasonable extensions, not directly sourced — those are marked with an asterisk.
Injuries
what's sore, how long it lasts, and what it changes
Log what hurts, 1–10. Severity is how long it lasts, not how much it changes your training: it decays at a rate the type sets and stops counting at 3, so a general 7 runs about two and a half weeks and a 4 about six days — tendinopathy longer, a sprain or strain shorter. How much it flares under load is what changes the session. High swaps the movement out, moderate takes a set off it, low leaves the plan alone. The warm-up targets the area either way, and running scales back on severity.

The engine
Why the score moved
every recomputation this visit, and what changed with it
▾
Blind days
the only way to know the score is telling the truth
▾
Every readiness score ever shipped is unvalidated, and part of the reason is that seeing one changes what you do — a deflated number measurably worsens mood and performance. One training day a week, picked at random and locked in before it arrives, the number is held back until the session is logged — which makes that day’s result an honest label rather than a self-fulfilling one. The difference between your blinded and unblinded days is your own placebo effect, and no wearable company has ever published theirs.

1. Who We Are

[APP NAME] is operated by [COMPANY NAME] ("we," "us," "our"). This Privacy Policy explains what data we collect, why, and what rights you have over it. It should be read alongside our [Terms and Conditions].

2. 🔴 What Data We Collect

Data you provide directly:

  • Account information (email, [name if collected])
  • Training data: logged exercises, sets, reps, weight, running distance/pace
  • Recovery data: sleep duration/score, HRV, resting heart rate, subjective soreness/mood ratings
  • Injury data: body part, severity, irritability, movement restrictions, notes
  • Goals and preferences: training days, session length, target exercises/weights, mobility self-assessments

Data from third-party integrations (if you connect one):

  • Oura: sleep, readiness, HRV, and related biometric data, as authorized by the specific permission scopes you grant during connection
  • Garmin: heart rate, sleep, steps, and activity data, as authorized during connection
  • *We only receive what these providers' own consent screens disclose to you at the time you connect — we do not have access to anything beyond the scopes you explicitly authorize.*

Data collected automatically:

  • Basic usage/device information (e.g., device type, app version) for debugging and reliability
  • [Add analytics tooling here once chosen — this section needs to match whatever you actually implement, not describe generic analytics you haven't built]

We do not collect: [payment card details — Stripe handles this directly and we never see your full card number], [location data, unless/until a feature requires it — update this if that changes], [anything beyond what's listed above — keep this section honest and current as the app evolves].

3. Why We Collect It

We use your data to:

  • Operate the App's core function: generating training recommendations based on your logged history, recovery state, and injuries
  • Sync data from connected third-party devices, when you've authorized that
  • Process your subscription payment (via Stripe)
  • Communicate with you about your account, billing, or material changes to the Service
  • Improve the App's recommendation logic over time — 🔴 *if this involves using aggregated/anonymized user data to refine the algorithm across all users (not just your own account), that needs to be disclosed explicitly and separately here, since that's a materially different use than "personalizing your own recommendations."*

We do not sell your data. We do not use your health data for advertising or share it with advertisers.

4. 🔴 How We Share Your Data

We share data only in these circumstances:

  • **With service providers who help us operate the App** — e.g., our hosting/database provider, Stripe for payments. These providers only receive what they need to perform their function and are contractually bound to protect it.
  • **With Oura/Garmin, in reverse** — if you disconnect an integration or take an action within the App that they need to know about, only to the extent our partner agreement with them requires.
  • **If required by law** — e.g., in response to a valid subpoena or legal process.
  • **In a business transfer** — if [COMPANY NAME] is acquired or merges with another company, your data may transfer as part of that transaction, subject to this policy or a comparably protective one.

We do not otherwise share, sell, or rent your personal or health data to third parties.

5. Data Retention

We retain your data for as long as your account is active, plus [X days/months] after account deletion to allow for recovery of an accidental deletion, after which it is permanently removed from our systems — except where we're required to retain it longer for legal or accounting purposes.

6. 🔴 Your Rights

Depending on where you live, you may have the right to:

  • Access the personal data we hold about you
  • Correct inaccurate data
  • Delete your data ("right to erasure")
  • Export your data in a portable format
  • Withdraw consent for a specific data use (e.g., disconnecting a third-party integration)
  • Object to certain processing
This section needs real legal tailoring depending on your actual user base's location — GDPR (EU/UK users), CCPA/CPRA (California users), and other regional frameworks each impose specific, different obligations (like required response timeframes, specific notice language, and in some cases a formal Data Protection Officer). A generic "you have rights" paragraph is not sufficient on its own once you have real users in these regions.

To exercise these rights, contact us at [privacy@yourdomain.com]. We use industry-standard measures to protect your data, including encryption in transit and at rest, and access controls limiting who can view your data internally. No system is perfectly secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security — if we become aware of a breach affecting your data, we will notify you as required by applicable law.

The App is not intended for use by anyone under [16/18 — match whatever age you set in the Terms]. We do not knowingly collect data from children under this age. If we learn we've collected data from a child without appropriate consent, we will delete it.

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. We'll notify you of material changes by [email / in-app notice] before they take effect.

11. Contact

Questions about this policy or your data can be sent to [privacy@yourdomain.com].

What I'd flag as genuinely non-negotiable before this goes live:

1. Section 2 needs to stay perfectly accurate to what the app actually collects — this document should be updated every time a new data type is added to the app, not written once and forgotten.

2. Section 6 is the one most likely to have real regulatory teeth depending on where your users are — this is where "close enough" isn't good enough.

3. Section 9 only matters once real hosting infrastructure exists, but needs to be revisited the moment it does, not left as a placeholder indefinitely.

4. This document assumes the in-app "Export All Data" / "Clear All Data" settings features (which already exist in the app) are the mechanism fulfilling the access/deletion rights in Section 6 — worth confirming that's still true as the app evolves, since a Privacy Policy promising a right the product doesn't actually deliver is worse than not promising it.
